`build-bootstrap.sh --tools` verifies/installs the public bootstrap as before,
then uses a small `TOWER_TOOLS_ONLY` CMake bridge to build the existing Tower
runtime binder, shared host runtime and `scaffolding/tools/build_tools.tower`.
Tower owns both tool recipes, compiler/linker argv construction and process
execution. This bridge does not configure upstream LLVM sources or build a
successor compiler. It retains the current Linux x64/Docker bootstrap route;
the installer and wider shell/CMake migration are still unfinished. The new
bridge adds 31 CMake lines and extends the existing shell entry, so deletion of
two Python files is not a claim that all non-Tower build glue is gone.

`tool_process_linux.tower` uses the explicit Linux pipe2/fork/execv/waitpid ABI,
with a close-on-exec errno pipe to distinguish launch failure from exit 127.
Reads, writes and waits retry EINTR; the parent joins the child on ordinary
error paths. Arguments borrow stable NUL-terminated strings synchronously;
there is no PATH search, shell interpretation or output capture. Exit codes and
signals remain distinct structured results; the command adapter preserves
ordinary status and uses 128 plus signal for signaled children. Build tools
stop before linking after compiler failure, emit import depfiles, and rebuild
their small objects on each call. No caching or parallel scheduling is claimed.
Output checks reject input/output and output/output symlink aliases before
compilation. They do not identify hard links or prevent filesystem races.

#### User direction: unified core vectors, swizzles and automatic SIMD

The user explicitly requested core float3/float4-style values, tentatively named
`f32_3`/`f32_4`, unified with Burst-style SIMD use and shader vectors, available
on CPU and GPU with swizzles throughout. They prefer the compiler to choose SSE
or other vectorization without requiring users to write manual intrinsics, and
remain open to a clean naming/model proposal. Recorded this as language direction
in docs/tower-language-plan.md, not as an implemented feature or finalized syntax.

The proposed common model is fixed-size logical lane values, with convenient
ordinary aliases over a type-producing application such as `vec(f32, 4)`.
The existing growable `vector(T)` is a different storage/ownership abstraction.
Neither a source value's lane count nor its memory layout should be defined by
the CPU's physical SIMD register width. The same entities/operations can be
scalarized, lowered to eligible CPU SIMD, or emitted as shader operations.
Auto-vectorizing multiple loop iterations uses the same arithmetic plus proven
alias/effect/access information. It does not imply arbitrary AoS/SoA rewriting,
automatic parallel threads, or equivalence to GPU subgroup lanes.

Proposed swizzle contract: `.xyzw`/`.rgba` on numeric and mask vectors; repeated
read selectors; unique writable lanes; one destination evaluation and a complete
right-side snapshot before overlapping writes. Include masks/select/any/all,
explicit conversion/splat rules and standard vector math. Decide equality,
normalization of zero, division/masking behavior and reduction order explicitly.
Strict staged arithmetic and runtime arithmetic must agree; SIMD reassociation
or approximate math cannot silently change that profile. Keep one canonical
Foundation spelling and shared ECS checking/lowering, with worker-owned scratch.

Primary references consulted:
[Unity Burst vector types](https://docs.unity.cn/Packages/com.unity.burst%401.4/manual/docs/CSharpLanguageSupport_Types.html),
[LLVM loop and SLP vectorization](https://llvm.org/docs/Vectorizers.html), and
[WGSL vector layout](https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#alignment-and-size).
These support the distinction between user vector values, vectorizer decisions
and explicit buffer layouts. In particular, WGSL's three-component vector size
and alignment differ; blindly adopting a SIMD register size is not interoperable
layout. Backend legality must cover SPIR-V/Vulkan, DXIL and direct WGSL/WebGPU,
including unsupported element types and optional capabilities. This is a design
proposal informed by those sources, not a claim of identical target behavior.

Plan vectors alongside the floating-point milestone, preserving the requested
remaining C-level work. First establish scalar numeric semantics, then shared
fixed-vector types/operations, swizzle sequencing, canonical/interpreter tests,
and target implementations with actual instruction/performance evidence. CPU
shader reference execution and shared ocean-wave/buoyancy math remain motivating
examples. No implementation, bootstrap change or todo.txt edit accompanies this
direction entry; all future implementation/tests remain Tower source.

#### Proposed next third-party port: WebAssembly linking

User asked which third-party dependency should follow the owned C/C++ retirement.
Recommendation, not an implementation or new active port: start with the LLD
WebAssembly functionality required by Tower's real programs and browser compiler
self-builds. Current backend/linker.tower owns the plans, but linker_wasi.tower
and linker_wasi_wasm.tower still bind lld::wasm::link and CommonLinkerContext via
the C++ ABI. Native cross-linking additionally uses ELF/COFF/Mach-O implementations.
LLD is several format-specific linkers and depends on LLVM object/support/LTO
machinery; translating its driver alone would not remove those dependencies.

First audit actual object/archive inputs, relocations and flags; implement a
bounded Wasm object and ar archive reader, symbol/type resolution, archive member
selection, relocation/layout and module writing in Tower. Preserve imports,
exports, initializers, tables, memory limits/alignment, weak/duplicate/COMDAT rules,
feature checks and diagnostics as exercised by those inputs. Shared-memory/TLS
requirements of existing threaded builds need an explicit gate, not an assumed
consequence of linking a tiny unthreaded example. Dead-section elimination is
link-time reachability, unrelated to a runtime garbage collector. No new public
semantic IR: linker section/symbol indexes describe platform objects and should
use shared world ownership where useful, with dense records for bulk processing.

Parallelize independent input decoding and relocation over disjoint output
ranges; coordinate deterministic symbol selection/layout and publish after joins.
Use upstream wasm-ld as the differential reference until real programs, both
serial/shared-worker compiler packages and two compiler generations pass. Compare
execution, imports/exports, diagnostics, determinism, time and memory; equivalent
linkers need not produce byte-identical layouts. Reject unsupported inputs clearly.
The first useful release excludes general LTO/dynamic-linker compatibility unless
the audited production inputs require it. Native ELF linking for the Linux/Docker
bootstrap is the next candidate, followed by required COFF/Mach-O coverage. LLVM
code generation remains external; removing wasm-ld alone does not make the compiler
free of native third-party implementation or establish a measured bundle speedup.

Sources reviewed: https://lld.llvm.org/ (separate linkers, LLVM object/LTO dependency),
https://lld.llvm.org/WebAssembly.html (link behavior and exports/imports),
https://github.com/WebAssembly/tool-conventions/blob/main/Linking.md (object,
symbol, relocation and target-feature contracts), and the pinned LLVM19.1.1 driver
https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/llvmorg-19.1.1/lld/wasm/Driver.cpp.
Current upstream documentation is design context, not an automatic upgrade of the
pinned LLVM contract. This entry changes no compiler implementation or bootstrap;
the existing tooling agent remains independent and todo.txt is untouched.
## 2026-11-21 - Playground cold and warm latency regression

Pulled through d2d5633 before implementation, retaining the user's uncommitted
todo.txt bytes. Git's automatic repack delayed the first pull; stopped only that
maintenance process and completed ordinary pulls with maintenance.auto=false and
gc.auto=0. No force push or feature branch. The new KnownProof/KnownClone,
aggregate-preparation and query-read work remains intact.

On Windows, AMD Ryzen 9 5900HX, Node 21.7.3 and Playwright Chromium, the live
playground reproduced the complaint. Two new-project clicks after a completed
program took 2636/2668 ms to highlight, 6336/6378 ms to graph output, and
8495/8548 ms to all selected outputs. Repeated Execute on the same project took
113/133 ms. Ordinary edits highlighted in 236/329 ms; syntax-only trailing edits
took 235/240 ms. These are measured browser actions/result DOM mutations, not
physical display latency. Live report: build/latency-live-before.json. That first
probe excludes the preliminary isolation reload from its cold navigation number;
the revised profiler records the original navigation across that reload.

Root causes: selectProject unconditionally terminated the parser and all idle
execution workers, losing warm module/grammar/compiler state on every project.
Ordinary edits also imposed a 200 ms delay before parsing and killed an in-flight
parser, despite the existing generation/coalescing protocol. Canonical operations
repeatedly fetched tower.tower even inside a warm worker. These browser boundary
policies now retain idle workers, replace complete project source capabilities,
coalesce stale parser requests, schedule highlighting on the next frame, and cache
bundled language-source fetches. The separate execution debounce and diagnostic
visibility policy remain explicit. Active execution/project/compiler cancellation
still terminates the affected workers, including nested workers.

CPU sampling of the current compiler independently found expensive sorted LR item
insertion/memmove and per-symbol rescans of entire LR(1) closures. New Tower-owned
closure-local hash indexes append unique exact items, preserve the pending stack
order, and heap-sort once before publication. LALR preparation scatters the sorted
closure once into outgoing kernels, preserving terminal-range containment and
nonterminal order. These are derived worker-private indexes, not new semantic
nodes or a replacement for ECS scheduling. Existing CompilerWork dispatch, joins,
world ownership and deterministic publication remain unchanged.

## 2026-11-21: Tower bootstrap packaging and in-house archive/hash capabilities

The tooling lane replaces the required `bootstrap/package.py` entry point with
`scaffolding/tools/package_bootstrap.tower`, built by the established
`playground/scripts/build-bootstrap.sh --tools` path. The independent installer
remains unchanged for this milestone. The user clarified that actual source
should become overwhelmingly Tower, with essential platform/browser bindings,
and subsequently prioritized eliminating Python completely before the wider
shell/CMake/JavaScript migration. This is actual implementation retirement,
separate from GitHub recognizing Tower in its language chart. This lane has now
removed four Python files (23 initially, 19 remaining; 147 lines in those four
files) and two obsolete JavaScript probes (94 lines). Three Python replacements
are live tools; the fourth removal was the obsolete grammar-port profiler.
Other concurrent source changes are not attributed to this lane's totals.

Architecture and contracts:

- New `library/sha256.tower` implements FIPS 180-4 SHA-256 with explicit bytes,
  wrapping u32 arithmetic, incremental updates and non-consuming finalization.
  It rejects a null nonempty input or a message reaching 2^64 bits before changing
  state. Specification constants are decoded from hexadecimal text once per
  initialized state because the public bootstrap lacks hex integer literals.
  This is an implementation with differential evidence, not FIPS certification.
- `tar_archive.tower` writes deterministic regular-file POSIX ustar, and
  `gzip_archive.tower` frames the existing Tower CRC32/DEFLATE compressor. File
  order is explicit, ownership/time fields are zero, modes are 0644 or 0755, and
  the gzip timestamp is zero with OS 255. No zlib, native crypto or tar library
  was added. The packager executable's `ldd` lists only libc plus loader/vDSO.
  The compiler being packaged still has existing LLVM transitive dependencies,
  including libz; this milestone does not remove LLVM's dependency closure.
- The small writer rejects unsafe/duplicate/file-parent-colliding names,
  unsupported ustar name splits, modes, sizes and padded output limits. It has
  no PAX, link-member, base-256 or extraction implementation. Buffers publish
  atomically and allow input aliases. Package input/padded tar is capped at
  1 GiB; memory includes inputs, tar and compressed buffers. These are initial
  reusable capabilities, not a claim of a complete archive library.
- Linux tooling exposes file type, bounded reads, lexical resource traversal,
  child stdout capture and no-replace directory publication. File symlinks keep
  their lexical member names and read targets; directory symlinks are skipped.
  Directory recursion is bounded at 128 levels. `statx` and `renameat2` are
  explicit Linux x64 capabilities. Child stdout uses an anonymous temporary
  file, avoiding pipe-buffer deadlock; the 64 MiB capture bound limits published
  memory, not temporary disk writes. Stderr is inherited. Exit, signal, exec and
  redirection failures remain distinguishable in the process result.
- The new CLI is `package_bootstrap COMPILER PREDECESSOR REPOSITORY
  NEW_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY BUILD_COMMAND [GIT LDD]`. It publishes a complete new
  candidate directory by atomic no-replace rename; it never overwrites the live
  pin. The manifest retains schema, archive/member/source/predecessor hashes,
  member sizes, revision and optional source patch. Git/ldd are explicit trusted
  executables, defaulting to `/usr/bin/git` and `/usr/bin/ldd`, without a shell.
  Build command is recorded provenance supplied by the caller, not execution or
  independent attestation. Inputs must remain unchanged during packaging, and
  staged new files are needed for Git to include them in source provenance.

Research used the primary [SHA-256 specification](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.180-4.pdf),
[gzip format](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952) and
[Linux statx interface](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/statx.2.html).
Independent GNU tar/gzip, sha256sum, and the unmodified Python packager/installer
were reference tools, not new project-owned implementations or test helpers.

Trials, findings and corrections:

- SHA-256 standard empty/abc/56-byte/112-byte vectors, every chunk split,
  million-`a`, continuation after finalization, null and overflow rejection pass.
  260 generated binary fixtures (lengths 0 through 259) agree with system
  `sha256sum --quiet -c`; per-byte and whole-buffer Tower hashing also agree.
  The first 112-byte expected digest had a transcription error (65 hex digits).
  Corrected the test data and added a length guard; this was not an algorithm
  defect. Initial packager draft syntax errors were fixed before execution.
- Archive fixtures cover empty data, a 513-byte binary boundary, UTF-8 names,
  the 155-byte-prefix/100-byte-name boundary, executable permissions, aliasing,
  complete padding bounds and failed-output preservation. GNU tar extraction
  followed by `diff -r expected actual` passes; `bin/runner` mode is 755 and
  `gzip -t empty.gz` passes.
- Initial raw-tar comparison differed at the header checksum and device fields:
  Tower wrote octal zero device numbers while Python leaves those fields empty
  for regular files. Both readers accepted it; retaining empty device fields
  now produces byte-identical raw tar for the real 34-member compiler package.
- Initial patch hashes differed between the checkout and isolated reference
  clone because Git selected eight versus seven abbreviated object digits.
  The tool now requests full object IDs, no color, no external diff and no
  textconv. Applying its patch in the clone and regenerating with the same Git
  flags produces identical patch bytes. Manifest dependency observations omit
  nondeterministic terminal ASLR addresses while preserving names/paths.
- Large binary process capture (131072 bytes), capture-limit rejection, child
  exit propagation, invalid descriptor EBADF, ordinary exits/signals/exec
  failures and exact arguments pass. Filesystem tests verify bounded reads,
  regular-file aliases, skipped directory/dangling resource symlinks, and
  no-replace publication against files, directories and dangling symlinks.
- CLI attempts with an existing output, missing resource directory, failed Git
  and missing ldd return failure. Failed attempts publish no candidate; existing
  candidate archive/manifest remain byte-identical. Failed publication can leave
  newly created parent directories, but never a partial authoritative candidate.

## 2026-11-21: ECS architecture assessment, known-input queries and worker refill

The architectural objective remains one authoritative entity/component model and
dependency-driven execution. Archetypes can improve homogeneous traversal, but do
not by themselves make irregular dependency walks parallel or fast. Schedule the
ready frontier, suspend consumers on missing inputs, share producers and detect
cycles; do not assign fixed dependency chains to threads. Keep nominal structural
publication explicit. Tiny jobs, excessive archetype transitions, broad barriers
and repeated full-world scans can outweigh parallelism. Judge progress by useful
work and end-to-end latency/throughput at increasing worker counts, not occupied
cores or the fraction of functions named ECS. Existing overlap/determinism checks
are correctness evidence, not a whole-compiler scaling benchmark.

Primary references reviewed: rustc's [overview and query architecture](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/overview.html),
[parallel compiler discussion](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/parallel-rustc.html),
LLVM's [ThinLTO design](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/ThinLTO.html), and
[Flecs systems/staging](https://www.flecs.dev/flecs/Systems.html#staging).
Rust documents demand-driven queries; its parallelism page explicitly warns that
parts are outdated, so it is not evidence for current default threading settings.
ThinLTO separates combined summary analysis from parallel backend work. Flecs
defers structural mutations and merges them at synchronization points; direct
component payload access still needs ownership. These support the design rationale,
not a claim that production compilers generally use Flecs or that Tower will
outperform them without measurements.

Implemented KnownInputs on the existing per-function SemanticKnownWork components.
Mutation and ordering jobs publish their facts, then complete KnownProof; parallel
input-eligibility jobs depend on that proof and own their traversal scratch. The
coordinator publishes selected candidates in source order and records each
KnownClone query's eligibility dependency. Eligibility still checks mandatory
inputs only; values and conditional control flow execute through the ordinary
interpreter. No separate folding evaluator was introduced. Candidate components
are reused between scan and eligibility rather than rebuilding another graph.

Native incremental build and the focused `known` suite pass with public bootstrap
2292bd8 (ecs-known-inputs-retry.log / ecs-known-inputs-tests.log). The initial build
correctly rejected an aggregate foreach copy; corrected it to the documented
borrow form `foreach (var &candidate ...)` with an explicit value assignment.
The suite covers graph/fast execution, target pointer widths 4/8, canonical output
at 1/2/4/8 workers, effects, lazy captures, dependencies and negative cycles.

The follow-on known-analysis scheduler now refills a free slot on each completion
instead of waiting for the slowest member of a fixed batch. Workers copy a frozen
context descriptor prepared before dispatch, avoiding reads of the coordinator's
changing scheduler descriptor. Task lookup storage and the completed body/value
states read by these kernels stay fixed. The coordinator records joined receipts
and releases claims as jobs complete; semantic patches and candidates remain
private until all readers join, then publish in source order. The native `known`
suite passes again (ecs-known-refill-build.log / ecs-known-refill-tests.log).

The same improvement is under validation for type layout: publish a completed
layout under its exclusive query claim, release dependents immediately and refill
available slots. Independent kernels keep running under the pinned entity view.
Collect failures and choose the earliest deterministic query-discovery ordinal
after draining ready work, rather than letting completion timing pick an error.
This removes the bounded-batch result vector. It is not yet a measured speedup.
AGENTS now calls out frozen context descriptors and avoiding unnecessary batch

Confirmed the native backend registration race in upstream LLVM source:
`llvm/MC/TargetRegistry.h` explicitly requires callers to exclude registry access
during registration, and its RegisterMC* helpers assign function pointers even on

thread-safety guarantee. backend_open and disassembly previously repeated target
initialization. Implemented Tower adapters for Linux pthread_once, Darwin
dispatch_once_f and Windows synchronous InitOnceBeginInitialize/InitOnceComplete;
WASI backend reactors retain one execution owner per isolated instance. Target
selection lists now implement backend_register_targets behind those adapters.

compiler thread entry exports. No C/C++ implementation was introduced.

The first build correctly rejected an initialized mutable module global in a
library. Ordinary uninitialized global storage lowers to LLVM undef, so dropping
the initializer would not establish a valid once predicate. Instead extended the
existing Tower runtime binder with an explicit backend-registry object profile:
one zero-initialized, pointer-aligned target word and an accessor. Native OS APIs
own that word; the isolated WASI instance uses it as its private readiness flag.
This is target/platform object production, not a new Foundation initialization
rule or constant evaluator. The binder also handles an unused declaration removed
by LLVM optimization by emitting the requested accessor directly.

calls; no completion may return before release, and exactly one entry/completion
pair must be observed. This tests the production adapter without assuming zero

## 2026-11-21: Tower bootstrap installer implementation and reader validation

The next Python-first milestone implements `install_bootstrap.tower` and shared
JSON/DEFLATE/gzip/ustar readers. This implementation checkpoint deliberately
precedes publishing its executable and switching the live wrapper: a fresh
checkout needs a Tower-built installer before it can unpack the compiler used
to build tools. The checked-in compiler archive remains the public 2292bd8 pin.

The new raw DEFLATE reader handles stored, fixed and dynamic Huffman blocks,
overlapping matches, the 32 KiB distance window and cross-block history. It
checks input extents, tree oversubscription/incompleteness, repeat counts, EOB,
reserved codes, backward distances and an explicit output bound. Gzip checks
optional headers/header CRC, trailer CRC/size and concatenated members, rejecting
trailing garbage. Output and consumed extent publish only after success. These
are buffered readers, not a streaming codec or a new zlib dependency. The
implementation follows format facts in [RFC 1951](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1951)
and [RFC 1952](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1952), without importing a native
codec implementation.

The JSON reader follows [RFC 8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259) with an
explicit strict profile: UTF-8 scalar strings, paired surrogate escapes and
unique decoded object keys. Nodes retain exact numeric source spans; unsigned
integer conversion is explicit and checked, never rounded through floating
point. Nodes/string storage/nesting have caller limits. Documents borrow their
immutable source and own decoded strings/nodes; parse failure leaves the prior
document intact. The regular-file ustar reader checks header checksum, member
bounds, portable UTF-8 paths, duplicates/file-parent collisions and zero end
blocks. Links, PAX/GNU extensions and base-256 numbers are explicitly unsupported.
The current pinned archive is within this supported format.

The installer reads schema 1 and the existing Linux x64 host profile, verifies
the compressed archive SHA-256, then matches every decoded member's name, size
and SHA-256 to the manifest before writing. It creates a private staging
directory, sets 0755 for towerc/0644 for resources, verifies the written files
and publishes with no-replace rename. A concurrent completed install is reused
only after verification. Cache verification opens each path component relative
to retained directory descriptors with O_NOFOLLOW, rejecting parent symlinks
as well as file symlinks. O_NONBLOCK prevents a substituted FIFO from hanging
before its non-regular type is rejected. The chosen cache root itself may be
resolved by the caller; member traversal never escapes it through symlinks.
Stage cleanup removes only validated member paths inside its own private
mkdtemp directory. No global recursive cleanup is used.

Limits are explicit: 1 GiB expanded data, compressed input allowance covering
the Tower writer's maximum stored-block overhead, 16 MiB manifest/string data,
65536 JSON nodes, depth 128 and 8192 members. The installer verifies expected
cache members; it does not claim an audit of unrelated extra cache files or
protection against concurrent mutation of the repository's source inputs.
The executable is Linux x64 and uses libc platform calls only.

Focused validation in the existing linux/amd64 `tower_build` Docker image and
private `tower_agent1_tooling` volume:

- `archive_decode_checks` compares 144 streams (four patterns, twelve boundary
  sizes, Tower output plus system gzip levels 1/9) against exact original bytes.
  It independently decompresses the actual checked-in pin with `/usr/bin/gzip`
  and compares the entire tar. All pass, including aliased inputs, output
  limits, every truncated short/dynamic prefix, checksum/size/header corruption,
  concatenation, reserved blocks, invalid backward distance, a one-symbol EOB
  with no distance alphabet, repeat-before-first and oversubscribed trees.
- `json_reader_checks` passes syntax/number/Unicode fixtures, escaped duplicate
  keys, u64 maximum/overflow, raw invalid UTF-8, document preservation and all
  resource limits, then parses the current real manifest. The initial test
  parameter name `expected` collided with Bedrock's token-mode keyword; renamed
  the test binding without changing compiler grammar or semantics.
- `tar_read_checks` passes regular-file reads, member limits, checksum/path/
  duplicate rejection, nonzero trailing data and explicit unsupported link and
  base-256 cases. Actual pin installation validates the real member set too.
- `bootstrap_install_checks` copies inputs into an isolated directory and
  passes fresh/repeated install, cache byte corruption, removed execute bit,
  equal-hash file and parent symlinks, FIFO, escaping archive symlink, damaged
  archive, invalid manifest and destination-symlink rejection. Rejected calls
  preserve the output path and a restored valid cache remains usable.
- Two concurrent installer invocations against a fresh shared cache both return
  the same verified path. This exercises concurrent use, without asserting both
  processes necessarily reached the publication rename simultaneously. The
  unchanged Python installer independently accepts that cache and its hashes.

## 2026-11-21: Superseding the installer with directly runnable bootstrap files

User steering changed the implementation decision: for **every** Python or
other-language script, first ask whether the step can disappear or be simplified
with existing capabilities; translate only the smallest required remainder.
Added that concise rule to AGENTS.md. The just-validated Tower installer is an
example of code we can avoid, so it is retired instead of becoming a new
bootstrap requirement. Its implementation and trials remain at 619b885 and in
the preceding journal entry. The initial installer executable was never pushed.

Caller audit found the default bootstrap wrapper was the only active installer
caller. The compiler already locates adjacent resources and runs from a relocated
directory. Therefore unpacking into a hash-addressed cache on every new machine
is unnecessary: check in that complete compiler directory and execute it there.
This preserves the single Linux x64/Docker bootstrap route without installation,
archive decoding, JSON parsing at startup, cache races or staging cleanup.

Final layout and retained contracts:

- `bootstrap/linux-x64/towerc` and its 30 accompanying resources/license are
  unpacked byte-for-byte from the existing 2292bd8 archive. Executable SHA-256
  remains `7ef1e6da14b9de1c5e06df2cc75ff8cb1058fb6ea5bd4c57a0a0f243ca28dc16`.
  The archive is removed; there is no new compiler build or semantic migration
  in this pin. Git records towerc as executable. Frozen resource attributes
  preserve exact bytes on Windows and identify them as generated distribution
  artifacts, not newly authored Tower/LLVM source for language-percentage claims.
- The existing shell boundary runs platform `sha256sum --check --status` over
  the 31-member SHA256SUMS file, checks the executable bit and returns the

  The explicit development compiler override still works. Broader upstream
  tools and CMake/shell entry points remain separate migration work.
- `development.json` schema 2 describes directory/executable/checksum-list
  paths; its top-level sha256 is the compiler hash. Existing member hashes,

  `archive_origin` records the previous archive hash/path as history. No other

- The infrequent publishing tool still needs to snapshot complete resources,
  source provenance and checksums. `package_bootstrap` now writes a directly
  runnable candidate directory, plain SHA256SUMS and schema-2 manifest using

### 2026-11-21 — scalar floating-point implementation, first arithmetic trials

Proceeding with scalar f32/f64 before fixed vectors and indirect calls. All new
implementation and tests are Tower. The ordinary integer-based functions in
library/float_bits.tower implement binary32/binary64 add/subtract/multiply/divide,
ordered/unordered comparisons, integer conversions and width conversion. Defined
rounding is nearest, ties to even, with gradual underflow and signed zero. Binary
arithmetic canonicalizes NaNs; copies/bit reinterpretation preserve payloads.
Negation flips the sign bit, rather than subtracting from positive zero. These
same functions serve staged evaluation, both interpreters and strict native/Wasm
runtime helpers. Hardware acceleration remains a later implementation choice;
this first strict path does not inherit ambient host rounding or flush-to-zero.

Reference reading: [SoftFloat arithmetic contracts](https://www.jhauser.us/arithmetic/SoftFloat-3/doc/SoftFloat.html),
[WebAssembly numeric execution](https://webassembly.github.io/spec/core/exec/numerics.html),
and [LLVM floating environment requirements](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html).
No external arithmetic implementation or new native source was added. Ordinary
LLVM floating arithmetic alone would not establish our stricter cross-host
contract, particularly NaN payload policy and ambient native floating environment.

Using the published predecessor through `/cache/values-tooling-clean/towerc` in
the Ubuntu/LLVM19 Docker validation container: tests/float_bits.tower compiles
and runs with zero failures. tests/float_reference.tower is a Tower generator of
independent LLVM fadd/fsub/fmul/fdiv reference cases. Its 10,240 deterministic
binary32/binary64 cases pass after NaN normalization (build/float-reference.log).
The generated LLVM is a test artifact, not project-owned C/Python tooling.

library/float_text.tower parses decimal significands as exact integer ratios and
rounds once at the destination width; it does not pass through host strtod or
binary64 for binary32 literals. Scratch is bounded local storage, with an explicit
4096-significant-digit diagnostic budget. Decimal output rounds exact expansions
to 9/17 significant digits for round trips. Initial halfway/subnormal/overflow
cases and 1,024 sampled round trips pass (build/float-text-tests.log: 0).

## 2026-11-21 - Tower static Wasm linker: first executable milestone

The user approved the proposed third-party port after 3b2e2bf. This entry
supersedes that entry's not-started status. LLVM code generation and production
LLD dispatch remain external/reference implementations; no dependency retirement
or full linker replacement is claimed yet. Pulled/rebased main through 6f73a74
before this batch, preserving the other tooling and browser work. No todo.txt
edits, new native code, sanitizer run or broad formatting sweep.

Implemented the port in new backend/wasm_*.tower modules: bounded LEB/UTF-8,
relocatable Wasm and GNU/BSD-name ar readers; symbol, COMDAT, target-feature and
relocation records; canonical type interning; strong/weak/local resolution;
reference wrapping; synthetic stack/memory/table/runtime symbols; root and
relocation liveness; deterministic function/global/table/data layout; typed
relocation patching; static module, export, element and constructor emission;
optional function names for diagnostics. Function/data relocation indexes are
CSR ranges, sorted only when necessary, with overlap rejection. Complete output
publishes only after success. There is no native linker call in wasm_link_run.

Each input and its layout are components on the same request-owned EntityStore.
Byte spans borrow immutable caller-pinned inputs; dense object records and derived
indexes describe platform objects, not another Tower semantic IR. World/type
identities never cross requests; pinned views prevent disposal. Current phases
are serial. The ownership and CSR layout prepare disjoint jobs, but are not
proof of parallel execution; worker overlap/cancellation gates remain work.
The standalone audit/static adapters and all new functional fixtures are Tower.
The only existing JS edit is a byte-source override in compiler-fixtures.mjs,
matching its existing TOWER_TEST_WASM override, to test an isolated LLVM reactor.

Primary contracts: WebAssembly/tool-conventions Linking.md and pinned local
LLVM/lld source at ~/.cache/tower/llvm-source-1e57ee22ca274b663eeb279fd86e7010a8441c99,
especially wasm/InputFiles.cpp, SymbolTable.cpp, Writer.cpp and Driver.cpp.
https://github.com/WebAssembly/tool-conventions/blob/main/Linking.md
https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/llvmorg-19.1.1/lld/wasm/InputFiles.cpp
https://lld.llvm.org/WebAssembly.html
The local source includes the existing SDK34 __wasm_first_page_end compatibility
patch. Optional runtime symbols preserve explicit target addresses; target layout
never comes from host sizeof. Explicit import-name metadata permits host imports,
including WASI, without broad allow-undefined. Ordinary unresolved strong
references fail; weak callable references use typed traps with null addresses.

Important rejected trial/correction: initial resolution produced eleven typed
signature variants in the LLVM archives. Reading all of SymbolTable's variant
code was insufficient: InputFiles first classifies FUNCTION_INDEX_LEB references
as direct calls. Address-only declarations (C++ vtables in particular) may carry
placeholder signatures and must keep the real definition/table address. The first
Tower-linked LLVM reactor instantiated but trapped inside TargetLoweringBase's
computeRegisterProperties when constructing the WebAssembly target. Added optional
Wasm names to identify the call, traced this to the overly strict variant policy,
and corrected it. The same archive inputs now require zero variants; direct-call
mismatches still get typed traps and two incompatible direct imports still fail.
New Tower fixtures distinguish these cases. Do not interpret the earlier eleven
variants as a required compatibility behavior. The fixed reactor passes actual
LLVM object/program generation and execution below.

Other findings: SDK34's __memory_base declaration can be mutable while the
published Tower compiler emits an immutable declaration. Static reserved base
symbols accept that declaration difference, keeping an i32 global with mutability
required by either input; unrelated global signatures remain checked. Strings and
retain segment flags are legal without merging strings; TLS remains rejected.
Padded signed relocation tests caught numeric convert on unsigned high bits;
bit reinterpretation plus explicit truncation now preserves i32/i64 patterns.
The public bootstrap silently rejects inline struct initializers passed directly
to inferred generic wasm_link_push; named typed locals avoid it without changing
the language. A temporary .tower bisection probe was removed. LLVM's object reader
also expects the name custom section before target_features; emission now follows
that order even though core Wasm permits custom sections more generally.

Reproduction environment: Windows/Node22.23.4, WSL Ubuntu, clang/LLVM19, WASI SDK34.
Documented build-bootstrap.sh selects the checked-in public2292bd8a compiler.
Isolated outputs are under ~/.cache/tower/coordinator-wasm-linker. For example:

    <public-bootstrap>/towerc scaffolding/tools/wasm_link_static.tower --library -o <cache>/wasm_link_static.o
    clang-19 <cache>/wasm_link_static.o <existing-Tower-build>/guest-host-library.o -o <cache>/wasm_link_static
    <public-bootstrap>/towerc scaffolding/tests/wasm_link_reader.tower --library -o <cache>/wasm_link_reader.o
    clang-19 <cache>/wasm_link_reader.o <existing-Tower-build>/guest-host-library.o -o <cache>/wasm_link_reader
    <cache>/wasm_link_reader

The existing runtime used was coordinator-retirement-handoff-clean/guest-host-library.o.

The support archives were decompressed from build/compiler-project/*.a.gz using
the existing gzip tool, not regenerated by a new helper implementation.

### 2026-11-21: simplify and migrate the live relocation verifier

The previous goal turn made progress by removing six unnecessary Python tools.
This turn's caller audit found verify-compiler.py still performs required real
CLI/relocation checks. Its only machine-readable report consumer was the inline
Python block in test-compiler-distribution.sh. Remove that JSON/report-parsing
step entirely: the Tower verifier now makes the expected-failure assertion
directly and writes plain command logs plus checks.txt. No JSON library or
second report validator is needed.

Implemented scaffolding/tools/verify_compiler.tower using the public checked-in
Linux x64 compiler and existing Tower byte buffers, file capabilities and SHA-256.
It retains help/options/version, missing-file and UTF-8 diagnostic location,
interpretation, three fresh byte-identical object emissions, separate library
linking, linked execution and three executable runs. Record compiler/object
hashes, exact quoted argument vectors, exit/process status, errno, millisecond
timings and separate binary stdout/stderr. Read bounds are 1 GiB per input and
4 MiB per log; they do not bound child disk writes. Every run requires a new
output directory and removes each object before the next compile, preventing
stale artifacts from satisfying checks. Failures retain their evidence.

The runner is explicitly Linux x64. Existing GNU env/timeout supply process cwd,
clean child environment (only the selected PATH) and the 180-second deadline plus
one-second kill grace. They are platform tools already in the canonical Docker
environment, not new installed libraries or an in-house process scheduler.
Commands use direct argv, never shell interpretation. Development mode permits
the caller's PATH; ordinary restricted mode permits only the compiler directory
and its tools child. The explicit expect_missing_clang mode requires the first
ten checks to succeed and then exact exit 1 plus the missing-Clang diagnostic at
link. It labels restricted release verification as NOT passed. Signals, timeout
and execution failures cannot satisfy a compiler-error expectation. Native
Windows/macOS release testing still needs its host runner and actual OS isolation;
restricted PATH alone does not prove portable dependency closure.

Extended the existing Linux process capability only enough to redirect stderr
independently while retaining child status and caller descriptor ownership.
Focused Tower tests cover distinct binary stdout/stderr including NUL, nonzero
exit, descriptor lifetime and stderr-redirection failure, alongside the existing
argument, signal, exec-error and large-capture/limit checks. All pass.

## 2026-11-21 - Independent body declaration frontiers and stable continuation order

The earlier body-frontier-next prototype is now implemented in the compiler;
this supersedes its uncompiled status in the local-query entry. Standalone local
declarations from the current body window bind in source order, release their
preparation claims, and enter one shared discovery/declaration executor. Each
producer retains its complete lexical continuation (scope, frame, defer/control
and flow state), so independent roots can advance through signature, inference,
field and layout dependencies together. Worker scratch retained by those lexical
continuations transfers to the coordinator after joining. The old one-body local
declaration helper is removed; nested control/protocol preparation still has its
separate structural continuation and remains unfinished migration work.

Failures belong to their producing query until a consuming body selects them.
The generic registry's sticky diagnostic is cleared only by the coordinator after
retaining the producer's error. Newly constructed types are associated with the
producer and contribute field/layout dependencies before that producer completes.
An unrelated later body's invalid layout therefore cannot select an earlier
body's error. Completed header/type checks are retained across readmission rather
than allocating parameter slots or checking initializers again. Explicit local
initializer finalization is still coordinator work where structural preparation
is required; this milestone does not claim all expression checking is parallel.

Review found another timing-sensitive boundary: layout workers continuously refill
and release declaration consumers in completion order. Structural continuations
can then register generated types/signatures. Added work_order_ready at this
joined boundary to restore stable coordinator request-ID order across the entire
ready frontier, including more than one admission window. It requires no running
tickets, removes consumed entries, and uses an allocation-free heap sort only
when the compacted queue is out of order. Ordinary scheduler dispatch stays FIFO;
task identity, access claims and stale-receipt checks are unchanged. The new Tower
work_order fixture completes 513 independent producers in reverse order, checks
FIFO before explicit ordering, yields a consumer, checks every ordered consumer
and stale receipt, and verifies exhausted-queue compaction. It runs through the
existing native/shared-Wasm work_pool fixture, without a new test tool.

## 2026-11-21 - Lazy Wasm libraries and an explicit Tower reactor link service

Continued the static-linker milestone after pulling main through 82dde6f. The
unfinished four-file archive change was stashed by exact path, rebased and restored;
no unrelated work was discarded. All new implementation and fixtures are Tower.
No todo.txt, native implementation, sanitizer run or broad formatter sweep.

Implemented indexed GNU archive extraction on request-owned archive components.
Original object/archive order is explicit; extracted object components retain
stable addresses while the coordinator publishes their derived resolution order.
A private iterative demand stack handles chained/backward references and cycles
without recursive host calls. Weak references do not pull members. Required and
optional exports are applied after ordinary inputs and can extract definitions.
This follows the pinned LLD Driver.cpp export handling and InputFiles.cpp COMDAT
rules, rather than assuming exports behave like initial undefined references.
COMDAT marking is shared with final symbol selection. A discarded member can
advance to another indexed candidate for the same name; empty symbol indexes are
distinct from missing indexes. Unused malformed members are not parsed. Thin and
BSD-index archives remain explicitly unsupported. Extraction is serial today;
world ownership and stable components alone are not a claim of parallel linking.

Moved option interpretation out of the executable into wasm_link_options.tower.
wasm_link_plan accepts borrowed, length-delimited argument/input spans with exact
name keys, including allow/export-list inputs. It performs no filesystem access.
backend_link_tower_wasm adapts existing BackendLink ownership, creates a fresh
world per invocation, and transfers only complete output. Failure clears output.
The existing reactor API selects it explicitly when argument zero is
`tower-wasm-ld`; ordinary `wasm-ld` keeps the upstream service. Unknown/unsupported
options fail without fallback. Planning errors remain blocking. The standalone
CLI is now a small file/argument/result adapter using that same decoder.

Integration exposed real duplicate-definition/type-boundary problems: importing
the entities, bytes and UTF-8 implementation modules into an already separately
linked compiler duplicated their exports. Old source/worker declarations also
erased entity parameters to void*. Mechanically moved the unchanged entity
layouts to entity_types.tower and added a typed entity_api declaration surface.

component layouts or lifetime rules changed. The linker now uses the shared ECS,
byte-buffer and UTF-8 interfaces, and standalone tools supply their implementations
once. Backend source roots and the LLVM worker convert opaque compiler handles at
the boundary and otherwise use concrete entity pointers. BackendLink types likewise
have one shared declaration module. Foundation and semantic algorithms are unchanged.

### 2026-11-21: complete byte/short scalar values in Tower

The user's next milestone follows published floats and integer negation. Pulled
main from cb1f340 to d5412d0 before editing, preserving the new structural-local
worker queries and Tower compiler-verification tool. Selected the remaining
i8/i16/u16 gap ahead of first-class functions: compact storage, binary formats
and ordinary foreign short/byte signatures benefit immediately. u8 already
existed. Foundation/Bedrock grammars are unchanged; ordinary type lookup receives
three new entries, with existing tags preserved. Compiler/runtime/tests are
Tower; small existing JavaScript ABI/version/fixture transports were extended.
todo.txt is unchanged.

Shared width, signedness, layout and unsigned-counterpart queries now cover all
integer widths. Exact signed-minimum magnitudes, logical right shift, checked
conversions and staged evaluation reuse the existing operations/interpreter.
No alternate constant folder, mutable cross-worker table or semantic IR was
introduced. The execution cache now has eight integer tags; its private opcode
layout and semantics versions advance to 4, container version stays 1. Canonical
Foundation remains authoritative and cache validation/reconstruction is required.
Native/Wasm signatures use the existing scalar ABI extension path, selecting
signext or zeroext consistently for calls/declarations/definitions. The LLVM
[parameter attribute contract](https://www.llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#parameter-attributes)
is the reference; actual cross-object Tower tests establish only the exercised
platforms, not universal C ABI compatibility.

The first new fixture failed eight short checks while every byte-pattern check
passed. A reduced output fixture showed two apparently equal i16 values comparing
unequal. Root cause: ix_load_size/ix_write_size had specialized 1/4/8-byte paths;
size 2 fell through into eight-byte access after validating only two guest bytes.
Added an exact two-byte early return in both shared paths. Explicit unaligned
neighbor-sentinel, array/struct/container and pointer-stride cases cover this.
Both graph and cached execution now agree on the full target memory image.
The exhaustive-byte fixture also exceeded old small-test replay budgets; bounded
round-trip/package replay now derives its budget from the completed graph run.
This was a harness limit, distinct from the memory defect.

LLVM reconstruction found a second pre-existing assumption: default<O2> in LLVM
19/20 resets loop/SLP vectorization options even after the C API disables them.
The narrow foreach reduction produced <2 x i16> on the intended scalar VM profile
and was correctly rejected by its scalar importer. Confirmed in upstream
PassBuilder.cpp (PTO assignments in the default pipeline parser) and vectorizer
sources. The private reconstruction profile now adds noimplicitfloat to its
functions, which the loop/SLP vectorizers explicitly honor for implicit SIMD.
It retains O2 scalar passes and strict floating helper calls. Native target
emission keeps its separate vectorizing pipeline; the same fixture's native
LLVM output contains a vectorized <8 x i16> reduction. This is an observed
eligible loop, not a general vectorization guarantee or a new public vector type.

C emission now uses width-driven signed decoding, checked conversion and division
overflow checks, with exact two-byte loads/stores and signed narrow signatures.
Roku already had generic masks/sign extension; corrected population counting to
include a partial 16-bit limb (also fixes its pre-existing byte case). The private
host text-print discriminator moved outside scalar tags to avoid colliding with
i8. Browser foreign arguments decode i8/i16/u16 exactly at the host boundary.

### 2026-11-21: profile and fix Tower linker overhead before further features

User reprioritized profiling/fixing the slowdown ahead of shared-memory/TLS or
parallel feature work. Keep the previous final generation's LLVM-reactor inputs
frozen under coordinator-wasm-linker/benchmark-memory and use the same argument
JSON/rsp. No source-generation/build activity overlaps the timing trials. WSL
does not have perf installed; install external Valgrind 3.26 and use only its
Callgrind instruction/call profiler, not a sanitizer or Memcheck. Command:
valgrind --tool=callgrind --callgrind-out-file=.../tower-baseline.callgrind
.../static-memory-final <benchmark args> -o .../profile.wasm, then
callgrind_annotate --auto=no --inclusive=no. The profiler reports a brk-growth
limitation; allocation continues and the image succeeds. Treat instruction
counts as attribution and measure actual speed separately without instrumentation.

Baseline: 3,173,339,567 executed instructions. Flat attribution: name insertion
14.42%, liveness/relocation indexes 12%, relocation emission 10.25%, relocation
record decoding 9.41%, name reading 7.23%, relocation-owner binary searches 5.15%.
The important repeated work is hashing a new name repeatedly and hashing every
stored name again during growth; searching each relocation's owner again in both
CSR passes; full UTF-8 decoding of long ASCII symbols; and decoding an existing
padded relocation operand whose value is immediately replaced.

Tower changes: retain a nonzero hash in the existing name-slot padding, compare
full bytes on hash collisions, reuse the first insertion probe and cached hashes
at growth. Empty keys/zero values remain valid. Object validation now retains one
derived u32 owner index per relocation; liveness consumes it directly. Consecutive
relocations try their previously validated chunk before the bounded binary-search
fallback, preserving shuffled-input and boundary errors. This is request-owned
derived indexing on the existing platform-object ECS payload, not a semantic IR.
ASCII validation skips eight bytes at once using an unaligned copy and an
endianness-independent high-bit mask, while non-ASCII still uses the same Unicode
decoder. Padded operand validation checks continuation/unused/sign bits directly
instead of calculating the discarded value; range checks and output encoding stay.

New Tower fixtures cover an actual full FNV collision (costarring/liquid), empty
keys, Unicode/truncated/invalid sequences across byte alignments, every last-byte
value for signed/unsigned 32/64-bit padded encodings against the ordinary decoder,
early terminators, reversed relocation order and chunk-boundary rejection. Native
suite passes. One initial fixture compile rejected the reserved word expected as
a local name; renamed it valid_encoding before running. No new helper scripts.

First three changes reduce instructions to 2,504,110,498; owner hints and direct
padded validation reduce them to 2,314,630,050 (27.1% below baseline). Original
and final images compare identical. Five uninstrumented baseline/final/LLD triples
in seconds: baseline 0.54/0.61/0.53/0.53/0.51; final 0.43/0.42/0.41/0.42/0.42;
LLD 0.46/0.46/0.42/0.44/0.43. Medians 0.53/0.42/0.44: about 21% faster than
previous Tower and 5% faster than LLD on this workload. Final RSS 351436-351660 KiB
versus baseline 344896-345160 and LLD 376380-376436. The retained owner indexes
cost about 6 MiB but remain about 6.6% below LLD. This supersedes the previous
slowdown observation for this frozen workload, not every linker/profile/platform.
Profiles tower-{baseline,indexes,final}.callgrind and all comparison images remain
in the isolated cache. Final Wasm and compiler-generation validation follows.

ordinary locations. No independent function-pointer instruction ABI was introduced.

#### Vector/shader requirements and ordinary scalar type definitions

User explicitly requires the coming f32_1/2/3/4 family to support compute and
other shader code, GLSL/HLSL-style generation and optimization, and eventual
SPIR-V integration. Recorded actionable tasks in docs/tower-language-plan.md,
without editing todo.txt. Preserve the existing DXIL and direct WGSL goals and
one shared ECS/Foundation semantic model. This entry records direction only.

Research check: Microsoft's HLSL vector documentation permits one through four
components. Base SPIR-V OpTypeVector requires at least two, while the optional
SPV_EXT_long_vector extension changes the one-lane rule. Therefore a portable
f32_1 must not accidentally depend on that extension: scalar lowering is the
baseline proposal. If f32_1 is a true f32 alias, it necessarily shares f32's type
identity and interface; any convenience .x/.r/swizzle behavior must be shared or
implemented through an explicitly distinct wrapper. That choice remains open.
WGSL's vec3<f32> example has size 12, alignment 16 and array stride 16: logical
lanes, CPU ABI, register width and shader-buffer layout are separate contracts.
References consulted 2026-11-21:
- https://registry.khronos.org/SPIR-V/specs/unified1/SPIRV.html#_type_declaration_instructions
- https://github.com/KhronosGroup/SPIRV-Registry/blob/main/extensions/EXT/SPV_EXT_long_vector.asciidoc
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/direct3dhlsl/dx-graphics-hlsl-vector
- https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#alignment-and-size

The user then asked whether i32 itself can be implemented in Tower. Current
implementation already writes scalar checking/layout, ordinary interpreter
arithmetic and LLVM lowering in Tower. It does not yet define i32 as an ordinary
library-produced type: foundation_tags has SI32; FoundationType has a scalar
tag; semantic_support recognizes signedness/width by those tags. backend_type
maps the checked width to LLVMIntTypeInContext. LLVM is a target implementation,
not the portable interpreter's type authority. The shared interpreter operations
also serve staged execution; replacing them with a second constant evaluator
would violate the intended model.

Proposed next architecture step to discuss before vector implementation: ordinary
Tower functions construct reflected scalar/vector type objects on the shared ECS
model; components describe representation, numeric semantics, layout and operation
implementations. Keep a small explicit foundation for bits/memory/control and
execution, with ordinary Tower definitions layered on it. A prior compiler builds
the next compiler, so self-hosted implementation does not imply infinite runtime
recursion or that the starting executable needs no machine primitives. Optimize
eligible operations to native LLVM/SPIR-V instructions under a verified semantic
contract; keep a portable interpreted implementation. Replacing built-in scalar
special cases, literal/default inference, canonical formatting and backend mapping
is incremental work, not an already available user-level integer-type API. No new
type-construction implementation is included in this discussion.

User priority clarification: ALL existing named types should have concrete Tower
source definitions, with dedicated modules such as i32.tower/f32.tower and Tower
implementations of pointer/reference, array, struct, enum, function and other type
constructors. Merely moving a special-case compiler switch into Tower does not
meet this goal. Shared generic implementation is welcome; dedicated definitions
need not duplicate arithmetic. Foundation includes/imports the standard types;
Bedrock remains the grammar/bootstrap layer and does not import that prelude.
The compiler's implementation types are distinct from Bedrock's user grammar.

### 2026-11-21: proposed relationship between attributes and type protocols

User asks whether attributes should express the common protocol for Tower-defined
types. Recommendation under discussion: define the protocol as composable typed
components on the existing type/operation entities, with ordinary Tower functions
implementing construction, layout, literal conversion and supported operations.
Attributes may attach those values and associate implementation functions; ordinary
type-construction code must be able to produce the same components directly.
This supports parameterized pointer/array/function/struct types without requiring
generated annotation text. Both paths share identity, checking, provenance and
compilable canonical Foundation rather than maintaining an attribute-only model.

An integer definition can supply width/signedness and arithmetic implementations;
pointer, aggregate and callable definitions supply their applicable capabilities.
Avoid a mandatory table of every possible operation for every type. Distinguish
metadata on a declaration/binding from metadata on its resulting type object:
aliases must not silently acquire different arithmetic or layout. Resolve ordinary
typed operations during compilation; a callback-based compiler protocol does not
imply guest runtime dispatch on each arithmetic operation. Backend implementations
must satisfy the operation's explicit semantics and target legality, not infer
correctness merely from an attribute name or matching storage width. Staging uses
the ordinary interpreter, with dependency queries and worker-owned output as before.

The minimum primitive execution/representation contract remains explicit. Attributes
do not remove bootstrapping requirements or make arbitrary annotations executable
compiler extensions. Implement the smallest typed metadata/protocol mechanism needed
for the standard-type migration, with attribute syntax over it where useful; this
does not require finishing every proposed reflection/attribute feature first.
This is a design proposal, not new syntax, a finalized API or implemented behavior.

### 2026-11-21: TLS and typed parallel relocation implementation

Implemented static wasm32 TLS layout/ABI globals, retained passive templates,
TLS offset relocations, per-instance initialization, padding clearing, mutable
TLS GOT updates and TLS-to-TLS pointer fixups. Ordinary shared data preserves
atomic once initialization. Invalid symbol/segment flags, signatures, TLS targets
and 32-bit addend overflow fail without publishing an image. Memory64/TLS64,
dynamic output and absolute shared TLS addresses outside TLS storage stay explicit
unsupported profiles. No Foundation operation or second semantic graph added.

Parallel emission reuses WorkGraph, per-request ECS job components, pinned views
and WorkPool. The now-public typed function values let WorkPool accept a kernel
without a native shim or dispatch ID. The coordinator freezes input/layout vectors
and output ranges; workers only copy/patch their range and private error component.
After draining, errors are selected in source order and output publishes atomically.
The pool is reused between code/data phases, with 256 Ki estimated cost grain
(bytes + 64 per relocation). Default remains one lane; --threads=N is an explicit
budget capped by actual transport capacity. Isolated backend reactors remain
single lane; native overlap is verified, not inferred from admission counters.
Cancellation is cooperative, coordinator-only, and not permission to mutate or
reenter a request. Both serial callbacks and parallel workers pin the owner;
admitted work drains before reclamation and a failed/cancelled image preserves
prior output. Input parsing/layout and individual kernels are not preempted.

The Tower-owned Bedrock seed now defines bracket attributes. Attribute, name,
string and integer arguments enrich the original parse entities through the
shared SyntaxNode component. Declaration attributes retain order, source spans,
formatting and structural equality. Initial grammar consumers support highlight

declaration attribute protocol. Bedrock does not acquire the standard-type prelude.

The declaration reader accepts the shared bracket delimiter, then classifies the

needed so future attributed ordinary declarations can share the delimiter.

is present, preserving mixed old/new declarations and canonical round trips.

Constructor continuation design needs one additional ownership distinction:
an instance's nominal type result must complete before its fields/layout, while
the originating declaration retains responsibility for newly created types'
validation. Carry that originating producer through nested constructor/alias
queries, attaching constructed-record work to it. Otherwise an alias to a record
with a recursive pointer can be turned into a false cycle by waiting for fields
inside the nominal-result receipt. Canonical instance interning should deduplicate
concurrent uses; syntax consumers depend on the instance result, and only storage
or the owning declaration waits for field/layout completion. This is a design
constraint for the next implementation, not a claim of completed constructor
scheduling.

### 2026-11-22: source-defined standard named types

User authorizes moving every existing standard named type into Tower source and
using ordinary compile-time execution for their construction. Pull main through
14ca673 before editing; this includes the latest declaration/body continuations,
streamed frontend/backend jobs and checked-in Tower composition units. Do not
modify todo.txt, introduce native/Python implementations or fork another parser
or evaluator. No named-type migration is claimed complete at this entry.

Implementation boundary: retain explicit primitive execution representations,
while standard names bind to type values constructed by source. Primitive type
values have checked, opaque execution representations and canonical constructor
spellings, never a public numeric type ABI. Type construction must run through
ordinary interpreter operations and dependency publication before consumers use
the resulting type. The initial audit covers all thirteen existing named scalar
types (bool, void, usize, i8/u8, i16/u16, i32/u32, i64/u64, f32/f64) plus the
metatype boundary. Pointers, arrays, records, enums and function signatures retain
their shared entity identities; source names must not become lexer keywords.

Start with representation constructors and type values, then source definitions
and their query scheduling/import activation. Validate an edited type definition
changing its actual representation, not merely a matching descriptor checked
against an independently hardcoded type. Bootstrap-compatible implementation
precedes adoption in compiler/build source; package complete resources and prove
a clean default successor before publication.

Implementation correction after the initial design trial: do not introduce a
new opaque metatype execution scalar merely to move standard names. The existing
type-constructor specialization path can publish transparent module type bindings
on the same KType nodes and declaration queries. Implemented `var Name: type =
TypeExpression;`, dedicated definitions for all thirteen scalar names, and
Foundation imports of the unchanged grammar module plus the type prelude. Removed
the ambient scalar-name creation loop. Explicit primitive representation
constructors select the existing integer/floating/boolean/empty/address kernels;
the standard files, not an independent registry, choose their representations.
This supersedes the earlier entry's proposed opaque runtime type-value design.
Arbitrary ordinary functions returning type values and computed type arguments
are still pending; no separate evaluator was introduced. Existing ordinary
`comptime` value operations work with these source-selected representations.

Type-name lookup follows unaliased type imports with cycle detection; ordinary
value imports retain their existing rules. Legacy files without imports acquire
a retained implicit Foundation import. Explicit grammar-only imports remain free
of ambient standard names. Canonical Foundation imports foundation_syntax and
uses explicit constructor spellings, including pointer_type/array_type, preserving
the representation when a familiar source name is rebound.

Experiments/root causes, Linux Docker tower-c-validation, LLVM 19:
- A forward alias initially let a checking worker recursively construct the
  alias while shared nodes were pinned. GDB stopped in sem_node through
  sem_constant_argument. Added alias producer edges to declaration discovery;
  construction/interner publication stays on the coordinator, and independent
  dependency discovery/consumers retain the existing isolated workers.
- Reusing KType.constant as a binding marker made generic inference mistake
  type arguments for integer values (`vector_dispose(&g.task_index)` could not
  infer T). Use KType.global for module type bindings; constant remains a value
  property. The compiler's semantic_types unit then compiled with the new prelude.
- Literal primitive parameters do not need template-value interning. Split
  argument validation from interning so ordinary pinned body workers can consume
  primitive representations without mutating the shared constant-argument index.
- A canonical array with a constructor base could not parse as an operand.
  Added functional pointer/array spellings through the same construction code,
  rather than widening Foundation into a general expression grammar.
- Built the bridge against the predecessor Foundation, restored the preserved
  new import wrapper, then built /cache/source-types-successor with the complete
  source prelude using /cache/source-types-bridge-fixed/towerc. Both builds pass.
  The temporary predecessor Foundation swap is restored; no source work was lost.
- `tower-execution-tests /work/scaffolding types` passes: graph/fast execution,
  32/64-bit targets, canonical stability, workers 1/2/4/8, alias cycles, malformed
  representations, enum/array/struct aliases and ordinary staged calls. A tracked
  virtual replacement of types/i32.tower with a signed 64-bit definition produces

### 2026-11-22: native ELF replacement plan

Pulled main through 47eef84. Begin with the existing static Linux x86-64/AArch64
download profiles: relocatable objects plus Tower's syscall runtime. Implement
checked ELF64 little-endian readers, world-owned input components, deterministic
symbol/archive resolution, section layout, target relocations and executable
emission in Tower. Reuse the existing byte/name/archive utilities and shared
WorkGraph/WorkPool, pin inputs before exclusive output jobs, join before error
publication. Keep the byte service independent of browser/CLI transport. Do not
claim dynamic host-compiler linking, native TLS or unimplemented relocations;
reject unsupported profiles explicitly. Remove the production ELF LLD binding
only after real x86-64/AArch64 output execution and differential tests pass.

References: System V [ELF header](https://gabi.xinuos.com/elf/02-eheader.html),
[symbol table](https://gabi.xinuos.com/elf/05-symtab.html), LLVM's
[x86-64 relocation IDs](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/llvm/include/llvm/BinaryFormat/ELFRelocs/x86_64.def),
and Arm's [AAELF64](https://github.com/ARM-software/abi-aa/blob/main/aaelf64/aaelf64.rst).
The attempted GitLab x86-64 ABI raw URLs returned 404; use installed upstream
LLVM relocation implementation and published ABI sources for cross-checks.
No new native/script implementation, no todo.txt edits, no sanitizer/format sweep.

Implementation now covers the static download profile in elf_{types,object,
link_world,link_symbols,relocate,link_jobs,link_emit,link}.tower and the ordinary
BackendLink adapter. Object/archive payloads belong to an explicit entity store;
symbol maps and section vectors are derived physical-link indexes, not compiler
IR. Retained object copy/relocation kernels declare immutable input reads and
exclusive output ranges through WorkGraph, use the existing WorkPool and keep a
world view pinned until every job is joined. Failures publish in input order.
Readers/symbol/layout publication remain coordinated; no parallel speedup claim.
GNU/BSD archive parsing and byte/name indexing reuse existing Tower utilities.

Production Linux plans now retain generated object bytes instead of temporary
files. Cross dispatch calls backend_link_tower_elf, removing lld::elf::link and
the cross reactor's lldELF dependency. COFF/Mach-O still use LLD. Native CLI host
compiler-driver linking and SDK/build linkers remain unchanged. This milestone
does not implement dynamic ELF/PIE, ELF TLS, IFUNC, init arrays, scripts, extended
section indexes, compressed sections or all relocation kinds; unsupported load

and array-count grammar with ordinary operands, leaving Foundation and Bedrock
unchanged. Numeric argument checking now suspends on an IntegerArgument query;
its typed expression is cloned and prepared by the existing staged-expression
workers and executed by the ordinary interpreter. The coordinator publishes
results before type interning. No arithmetic evaluator, native helper or new
implementation language was added. Generic numeric bindings also resolve as
typed value operands inside expressions, allowing T[count + 1] and primitive
representations such as integer_type(width * 2, 1).

### 2026-11-22 — Persistent body and lowering query continuations

Rebase this work onto cf6b204 and the published 18664657 Linux x64 development
bootstrap. Body admission/checking now retain their coordinator continuation on
the program entity. Bounded pumps return waiting without throwing away lexical
scratch, replaying checked statements or forcing unfinished headers. A blocked
256-body source window admits later producers; ready dispatch stays bounded.
The ordinary body entry point drains these pumps and services declaration and
already-demanded interpreter inputs before diagnosing a quiescent dependency.
Cycles use the shared graph; an acyclic unfinished producer has a separate error.

Discovery now selects all tickets before dispatch, freezes its context, joins
workers and publishes receipts before another phase runs. This fixes graph
mutation during discovery dispatch. Malformed bodies also use that worker path;
remove the obsolete whole-function serial checker and its structural adapter.
Aggregate preparation and expression lowering retain per-function work components
and expose bounded pumps, registering newly available bodies without replaying
published functions. Context disposal releases suspended work after pool shutdown.

Add a KnownSnapshot join over the existing immutability proof and inferred-value
clone queries. Lowering depends on that receipt instead of an implicit phase-order
assumption while expressions still borrow runtime nodes. The join is demanded
after clone producer registration, avoiding premature demand of unsealed work.
There is no new evaluator or initializer-as-constant shortcut.

/tmp/tower-home/.cache/tower/ecs-local-query-new-pin. query-smoke exercises the

header/body cycle, cancellation, malformed bodies and a ready 257th body beyond
a blocked window. All pass. control-smoke and type-smoke pass parsed programs,
canonical reparsing, serial/threaded behavior and ordered failures. The inferred
known-bindings fixture prints 0 through both interpreters. Small changed units
compile through the public bootstrap. Logs are body-pipeline-native.log,

pipeline-snapshot-native.log, body-admission-unified.log and body-window-query.log
under build/language-next-audit/. Initial focused builds caught missing direct

before the passing runs. No sanitizers or broad formatting passes.

### 2026-11-22 — Explicit language imports, example audit and inspection follow-ups

The user refined the no-import policy during implementation. Supersede the earlier
proposal to reject every import-free file with a Bedrock exception: every file
instead starts from the same immutable declaration seed. Bedrock is an ordinary
file that can redefine that grammar, and an unrelated language can do so under
any filename. No import is required for grammar-only source; ordinary executable
syntax and named types must come from explicit imports or local definitions.
Remove the implicit Foundation prelude and the host's invented dependency entries.
Keep the existing parser/semantic operations and shared graph as the authority.

Record a usability requirement: missing language syntax needs helpful import
errors, including `import tower;`, `import foundation;` and `import bedrock;`.
The initial diagnostic covers executable-looking input while only the seed is
active. Richer contextual suggestions, such as suggesting Tower when Foundation
does not recognize an expression operator, remain follow-up work. Do not reject
valid custom-language source merely because it has no imports.

The library tree must follow actual dependency completion order, including cached
imports and diamonds, rather than discovery order or a hardcoded Bedrock-first
sort. Use the compiler's existing module completion path and keep JavaScript as
transport. New Tower checks cover the cold/cached diamond order, a custom language
without imports, an empty file, and the initial missing-language diagnostic.

Audit all twelve bundled example projects. Ordinary programs retain Tower imports
and use direct conditions, nested expressions, inferred generic calls, compound
updates, counted loops and complete initialization where appropriate. Foreach,
increment, replacements and tokens remain grammar lessons. Explain collection
allocation in short comments: initialization is empty, stack growth uses realloc,
queue growth allocates/copies, failure preserves old values, and dispose frees
owned memory. Fix the raw memory example to retain its old pointer when realloc
fails and guard the first-element read if no append succeeded. Public-bootstrap
preflight runs of templates, memory, functions and collections produce their
expected outputs (build/example_audit_preflight.log). A trial using a captured
named capacity in a type argument was rejected by the current staging contract;
retain the four-slot fixture and infer only supported generic type arguments.

Investigated the Bedrock header comments. GrammarTemplate already is an ordinary
recursive parse rule, with nested braces and a contextual character fallback.
GrammarPattern is an ordinary contextual token that captures a delimited regex;
syntax_reader_token passes its interior span to the Tower regex implementation.
regex_grammar builds shared LR grammar entities over Unicode scalars and
regex_lowering derives the lexer automaton. This is not a host regex engine or
an independent handwritten brace scanner. A parse-rule pattern form is possible
in principle, but must preserve raw whitespace, escapes, character classes and
delimiter boundaries. The reader still expects delimiters around the captured
span, and syntax_session_scan marks GrammarPattern opaque for highlighting by
name. Journal that remaining special case rather than claiming arbitrary embedded
language syntax is already fully generic. Clarify both the Bedrock file comments
and the seed builder's matching comments; a larger lexical-boundary design is a
separate change, not required merely to rephrase these comments.

Additional requested inspection fixes: bracket attributes need highlighting,
specific hover information and tree-query presentation; integer_type and its
width/signedness arguments must not inherit the enclosing function's return
description. The latter is a general hover selection problem in type-function
bodies, not just one missing builtin description. Investigate the existing shared
attribute entities and generic inspection metadata, with all reusable behavior
and assertions in Tower. These requests remain in progress at this entry.

### Hosted ELF linker continuation plan (2026-11-22)

The completed byte-linker publication leaves hosted Linux CLI/LLVM-library link
steps using a compiler driver. Continue that boundary now, preserving hosted libc
semantics. Reuse ElfLink's object/archive entities, symbol/relocation records and
shared WorkGraph/WorkPool; shared-object exports are a new request-owned component,
not a second semantic graph. Parse explicit ELF64 DSOs, SONAME/default symbol
versions and dynamic symbols. Emit PIE interpreter/dynamic/hash/version/relocation
metadata, eager GOT/PLT bindings and protected RELRO without executable writable
segments. Resolve versioned imports deterministically and preserve weak references.

Keep the static freestanding service's bytes unchanged. Dynamic relocation plans
are coordinator-derived immutable metadata; ordinary workers retain disjoint
output writes and private diagnostics. The driver supplies OS startup objects,
libc and requested shared-library bytes explicitly. Reuse existing tool discovery
for Clang/runtime object generation, but do not ask a native linker to produce the
executable. Standard libc startup stays an external OS input, not an owned native
shim. Support current Linux x64/ARM64 target profiles and reject unsupported ABI
contracts explicitly. Validate libc argument/environment startup, allocation,
external data/functions, function addresses, versions, weak imports, exports,
archives, raw/optimized execution, malformed inputs and worker determinism before
changing defaults or bootstrap/build linking.

References: ELF gABI Dynamic Linking (https://gabi.xinuos.com/elf/08-dynamic.html),
upstream glibc elf.h/dl-version.c and x86_64/start.S, and Arm's aaelf64.rst.
Those specify file/OS contracts; implementation and functional fixtures remain
Tower. LLVM and platform libraries remain third-party inputs.

of a nominal identity whose fields have not checked yet. The recursive-record
